entries.2d4578d3dd694c9286fd6afe72096f99534e269a: <div sID="gen2589" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="Lev.23" sID="Lev.23"/> <div eID="gen2589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2590" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2591" type="x-p"/> Hitherto the levitical law had been chiefly conversant about holy persons, holy things, and holy places; in this chapter we have the institution of holy times, many of which had been mentioned occasionally before, but here they are all put together, only the new moons are not mentioned. All the rest of the feasts of the Lord are, I. The weekly feast of the sabbath, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.3">ver. 3</reference>. II. The yearly feasts, 1. The passover, and the feast of unleavened bread (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.4-Lev.23.8">ver. 4-8</reference>), to which was annexed the offering of the sheaf of firstfruits, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.9-Lev.23.14">ver. 9-14</reference>. 2. Pentecost, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.15-Lev.23.22">ver. 15-22</reference>. 3. The solemnities of the seventh month. The feast of trumpets on the first day (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.23-Lev.23.25">ver. 23-25</reference>), the day of atonement on the tenth day (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.26-Lev.23.32">ver. 26-32</reference>), and the feast of tabernacles on the fifteenth, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.33-Lev.23.44">ver. 33</reference>, &c.
entries.b34d90f83db18ac81bbce36bdcd708ffed2586fe: <div eID="gen2591" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2590" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sundry Feasts. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2592" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, <hi type="italic">Concerning</hi> the feasts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which ye shall proclaim <hi type="italic">to be</hi> holy convocations, <hi type="italic">even</hi> these <hi type="italic">are</hi> my feasts. 3 Six days shall work be done: but the seventh day <hi type="italic">is</hi> the sabbath of rest, an holy convocation; ye shall do no work <hi type="italic">therein</hi>: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the sabbath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in all your dwellings. <div eID="gen2592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2593" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general account of the holy times which God appointed (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.2">v. 2</reference>), and it is only his appointment that can make time holy; for he is the Lord of time, and as soon as ever he had set its wheels a-going it was he that sanctified and blessed one day above the rest, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.3">Gen. ii. 3</reference>. Man may by his appointment make a good day (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.19">Esth. ix. 19</reference>), but it is God's prerogative to make a holy day; nor is any thing sanctified but by the stamp of his institution. As all inherent holiness comes from his special grace, so all adherent holiness from his special appointment. Now, concerning the holy times here ordained, observe, 1. They are called <hi type="italic">feasts.</hi> The day of atonement, which was one of them, was a fast; yet, because most of them were appointed for joy and rejoicing, they are in the general called feasts. Some read it, <hi type="italic">These are my assemblies,</hi> but that is co-incident with <hi type="italic">convocations.</hi> I would rather read it, These are <hi type="italic">my solemnities;</hi> so the word here used is translated (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.20">Isa. xxxiii. 20</reference>), where Zion is called the <hi type="italic">city of our solemnities:</hi> and, reading it so here, the day of atonement was as great a solemnity as any of them. 2. They are the feasts of the Lord (<hi type="italic">my feasts</hi>), observed to the honour of his name, and in obedience to his command. 3. They were proclaimed; for they were not to be observed by the priests only that attended the sanctuary, but by all the people. And this proclamation was the joyful sound concerning which we read, <hi type="italic">Blessed are the people that know it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.15">Ps. lxxxix. 15</reference>. 4. They were to be sanctified and solemnized with holy convocations, that the services of these feasts might appear the more honourable and august, and the people the more unanimous in the performance of them; it was for the honour of God and his institutions, which sought not corners and the purity of which would be best preserved by the public administration of them; it was also for the edification of the people in love that the feasts were to be observed as holy convocations. <div eID="gen2593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2594" type="x-p"/> II. A repetition of the law of the sabbath in the first place. Though the annual feasts were made more remarkable by the general attendance at the sanctuary, yet these must not eclipse the brightness of the sabbath, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.3">v. 3</reference>. They are here told, 1. That on that day they must withdraw themselves from all the affairs and business of the world. It is a <hi type="italic">sabbath of rest,</hi> typifying our spiritual rest from sin, and in God: <hi type="italic">You shall do no work therein.</hi> On other holy days they were forbidden to do any servile work (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.7">v. 7</reference>), but on the sabbath, and the day of atonement (which is also called a sabbath), they were to do no work at all, no, not the dressing of meat. 2. On that day they must employ themselves in the service of God. (1.) It is a <hi type="italic">holy convocation;</hi> that is, "If it lie within your reach, you shall sanctify it in a religious assembly: let as many as can come to the door of the tabernacle, and let others meet elsewhere for prayer, and praise, and the reading of the law," as in the schools of the prophets, while prophecy continued, and afterwards in the synagogues. Christ appointed the New-Testament sabbath to be a holy convocation, by meeting his disciples once and again (and perhaps oftener) on the first day of the week. (2.) "Whether you have opportunity of sanctifying it in a holy convocation or not, yet let it be <hi type="italic">the sabbath of the Lord in all your dwellings.</hi> Put a difference between that day and other days in your families. It is the <hi type="italic">sabbath of the Lord,</hi> the day on which he rested from the work of creation, and on which he has appointed us to rest; let it be observed in all your dwellings, even now that you dwell in tents." Note, God's sabbaths are to be religiously observed in every private house, by every family apart, as well as by many families together in holy convocations. The sabbath of the Lord in our dwellings will be their beauty, strength, and safety; it will sanctify, edify, and glorify them.
entries.7579b4a0bf5b507f8301d2e59d16f13779977cd0: <div eID="gen2594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2595" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the feasts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">even</hi> holy convocations, which ye shall proclaim in their seasons. <hi type="super">5</hi> In the fourteenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the first month at even <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's passover. <hi type="super">6</hi> And on the fifteenth day of the same month <hi type="italic">is</hi> the feast of unleavened bread unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : seven days ye must eat unleavened bread. <hi type="super">7</hi> In the first day ye shall have an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein. <hi type="super">8</hi> But ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> seven days: in the seventh day <hi type="italic">is</hi> an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work <hi type="italic">therein.</hi> 9 And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">10</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye be come into the land which I give unto you, and shall reap the harvest thereof, then ye shall bring a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest unto the priest: <hi type="super">11</hi> And he shall wave the sheaf before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to be accepted for you: on the morrow after the sabbath the priest shall wave it. <hi type="super">12</hi> And ye shall offer that day when ye wave the sheaf an he lamb without blemish of the first year for a burnt offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">13</hi> And the meat offering thereof <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> two tenth deals of fine flour mingled with oil, an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sweet savour: and the drink offering thereof <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> of wine, the fourth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an hin. <hi type="super">14</hi> And ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God: <hi type="italic">it shall be</hi> a statute for ever throughout your generations in all your dwellings. <div eID="gen2595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2596" type="x-p"/> Here again the feasts are called the <hi type="italic">feasts of the Lord,</hi> because he appointed them. Jeroboam's feast, which he <hi type="italic">devised of his own heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.33">1 Kings xii. 33</reference>), was an affront to God, and a reproach upon the people. These feasts were to be proclaimed in their seasons (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.4">v. 4</reference>), and the seasons God chose for them were in March, May and September (according to our present computation), not in winter, because travelling would then be uncomfortable, when the days were short, and the ways foul; not in the middle of summer, because then in those countries they were gathering in their harvest and vintage, and could be ill spared from their country business. Thus graciously does God consult our comfort in his appointments, obliging us thereby religiously to regard his glory in our observance of them, and not to complain of them as a burden. The solemnities appointed them were, 1. Many and returned frequently, which was intended to preserve in them a deep sense of God and religion, and to prevent their inclining to the superstitions of the heathen. God kept them fully employed in his service, that they might not have time to hearken to the temptations of the idolatrous neighbourhood they lived in. 2. They were most of them times of joy and rejoicing. The weekly sabbath is so, and all their yearly solemnities, except the day of atonement. God would thus teach them that wisdom's ways are pleasantness, and engage them to his service by encouraging them to be cheerful in it and to sing at their work. Seven days were days of strict rest and holy convocations; the first day and the seventh of the feast of unleavened bread, the day of pentecost, the day of the feast of trumpets, the first day and the eighth of the feast of tabernacles, and the day of atonement: here were six for holy joy and one only for holy mourning. We are commanded to <hi type="italic">rejoice evermore,</hi> but not to be evermore weeping. Here is, <div eID="gen2596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2597" type="x-p"/> I. A repetition of the law of the passover, which was to be observed on the fourteenth day of the first month, in remembrance of their deliverance out of Egypt and the distinguishing preservation of their first-born, mercies never to be forgotten. This feast was to begin with the killing of the paschal lamb, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.5">v. 5</reference>. It was to continue seven days, during all which time they were to eat sad bread, that was unleavened (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.6">v. 6</reference>), and the first and last day of the seven were to be days of <hi type="italic">holy rest</hi> and <hi type="italic">holy convocations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.23.7-Lev.23.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. They were not idle days spent in sport and recreation (as many that are called Christians spend their holy days), but offerings were <hi type="italic">made by fire unto the Lord</hi> at his altar; and we have reason to think that the people were taught to employ their time in prayer, and praise, and godly meditation. <div eID="gen2597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2598" type="x-p"/> II. An order for the offering of a sheaf of the first-fruits, upon the second day of the feast of unleavened bread; the first is called the <hi type="italic">sabbath,</hi> because it was observed as a sabbath (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.11">v. 11</reference>), and, on the morrow after, they had this solemnity. A sheaf or handful of new corn was brought to the priest, who was to heave it up, in token of his presenting it to the God of Heaven, and to wave it to and fro before the Lord, as the Lord of the whole earth, and this should be accepted for them as a thankful acknowledgment of God's mercy to them in clothing their fields with corn, and of their dependence upon God, and desire towards him, for the preserving of it to their use. For it was the expression both of prayer and praise, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.11">v. 11</reference>. A lamb for a burnt-offering was to be offered with it, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.12">v. 12</reference>. As the sacrifice of animals was generally attended with meat-offerings, so this sacrifice of corn was attended with a burnt-offering, that bread and flesh might be set together on God's table. They are forbidden to eat of their new corn till this handful was offered to God; for it was fit, if God and Israel feast together, that he should be served first. And the offering of this sheaf of first-fruits in the name of the whole congregation did, as it were, sanctify to them their whole harvest, and give them a comfortable use of all the rest; for then we may <hi type="italic">eat our bread with joy</hi> when we have, in some measure, performed our duty to God, and God has accepted our works, for thus all our enjoyments become clean to us. Now, 1. This law was given now, though there was no occasion for putting it in execution till they came to Canaan: in the wilderness they sowed no corn; but God's feeding them there with <hi type="italic">bread from heaven</hi> obliged them hereafter not to grudge him his share of their bread out of the earth. We find that when they came into Canaan the manna ceased upon the very day that the sheaf of first-fruits was offered; they had eaten of the old corn the day before (<reference osisRef="Josh.5.11">Josh. v. 11</reference>), and then on this day they offered the first-fruits, by which they became entitled to the new corn, too (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.12">v. 12</reference>), so that there was no more occasion for manna. 1. This sheaf of first-fruits was typical of our Lord Jesus, who has risen from the dead as the <hi type="italic">first-fruits of those that slept,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">1 Cor. xv. 20</reference>. That <hi type="italic">branch of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Isa. iv. 2</reference>) was then presented to him, in virtue of the sacrifice of himself, the Lamb of God, and it was accepted for us. It is very observable that our Lord Jesus rose from the dead on the very day that the first-fruits were offered, to show that he was the substance of this shadow. 3. We are taught by this law to <hi type="italic">honour the Lord with our substance, and with the first-fruits of all our increase,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.3.9">Prov. iii. 9</reference>. They were not to eat of their new corn till God's part was offered to him out of it (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.14">v. 14</reference>), for we must always begin with God, begin our lives with him, begin every day with him, begin every meal with him, begin every affair and business with him; <hi type="italic">seek first the kingdom of God.</hi>
entries.0aba7ec52c4a1013934fbb5b5ca297e217a918a7: <div eID="gen2598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2599" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete: <hi type="super">16</hi> Even unto the morrow after the seventh sabbath shall ye number fifty days; and ye shall offer a new meat offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">17</hi> Ye shall bring out of your habitations two wave loaves of two tenth deals: they shall be of fine flour; they shall be baken with leaven; <hi type="italic">they are</hi> the firstfruits unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">18</hi> And ye shall offer with the bread seven lambs without blemish of the first year, and one young bullock, and two rams: they shall be <hi type="italic">for</hi> a burnt offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , with their meat offering, and their drink offerings, <hi type="italic">even</hi> an offering made by fire, of sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">19</hi> Then ye shall sacrifice one kid of the goats for a sin offering, and two lambs of the first year for a sacrifice of peace offerings. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the priest shall wave them with the bread of the firstfruits <hi type="italic">for</hi> a wave offering before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , with the two lambs: they shall be holy to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for the priest. <hi type="super">21</hi> And ye shall proclaim on the selfsame day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> it may be an holy convocation unto you: ye shall do no servile work <hi type="italic">therein: it shall be</hi> a statute for ever in all your dwellings throughout your generations. <hi type="super">22</hi> And when ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field when thou reapest, neither shalt thou gather any gleaning of thy harvest: thou shalt leave them unto the poor, and to the stranger: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <div eID="gen2599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2600" type="x-p"/> Here is the institution of the feast of <hi type="italic">pentecost,</hi> or <hi type="italic">weeks,</hi> as it is called (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.9">Deut. xvi. 9</reference>), because it was observed fifty days, or seven weeks, after the passover. It is also called the <hi type="italic">feast of harvest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Exod. xxiii. 16</reference>. For as the presenting of the sheaf of first-fruits was an introduction to the harvest, and gave them liberty to put in the sickle, so they solemnized the finishing of their corn-harvest at this feast. 1. Then they offered a handful of ears of barley, now they offered <hi type="italic">two loaves of wheaten bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.23.17">v. 17</reference>. This was leavened. At the passover they ate unleavened bread, because it was in remembrance of the bread they ate when they came out of Egypt, which was unleavened; but now at pentecost it was leavened, because it was an acknowledgment of God's goodness to them in their ordinary food, which was leavened. 2. With that sheaf of first-fruits they offered only one lamb for a burnt-offering, but with these loaves of first-fruits they offered seven lambs, two rams, and one bullock, all for a burnt-offering, so giving glory to God, as the Lord of their land and the Lord of their harvest, by whose favour they lived and to whose praise they ought to live. They offered likewise a kid for a sin-offering, so taking shame to themselves as unworthy of the bread they ate, and imploring pardon for their sins, by which they had forfeited their harvest-mercies, and which they had been guilty of in the receiving of them. And lastly, two lambs for a sacrifice of peace-offerings, to beg a blessing upon the corn they had gathered in, which would be neither sure nor sweet to them without that blessing, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">Hag. i. 9</reference>. These were the only peace-offerings that were offered on the behalf of the whole congregation, and they were reckoned <hi type="italic">most holy</hi> offerings, whereas other peace-offerings were but <hi type="italic">holy.</hi> All these offerings are here appointed, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.18-Lev.23.20">v. 18-20</reference>. 3. That one day was to be kept with a holy convocation, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.21">v. 21</reference>. It was one of the days on which all Israel was to meet God and one another, at the place which the Lord should choose. Some suggest that whereas seven days were to make up the feast of unleavened bread there was only one day appointed for the feast of pentecost, because this was a busy time of the year with them, and God allowed them speedily to return to their work in the country. This annual feast was instituted in remembrance of the giving of the law upon Mount Sinai, the fiftieth day after they came out of Egypt. That was the feast which they were told in Egypt must be observed to God in the wilderness, as a memorial of which ever after they kept this feast. But the period and perfection of this feast was the pouring out of the Spirit upon the apostles on the day of this feast (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.1">Acts ii. 1</reference>), in which the law of faith was given, fifty days after Christ our passover was sacrificed for us. And on that day (as bishop Patrick well expresses it) the apostles, having themselves received the <hi type="italic">first-fruits of the Spirit,</hi> begat three thousand souls, through the word of truth, and presented them, as the first-fruits of the Christian church, to God and the Lamb. <div eID="gen2600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2601" type="x-p"/> To the institution of the feast of pentecost is annexed a repetition of that law which we had before (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.9">ch. xix. 9</reference>), by which they were required to leave the gleanings of their fields, and the corn that grew on the ends of the butts, for the poor, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.22">v. 22</reference>. Probably it comes in here as a thing which the priests must take occasion to remind the people of, when they brought their first-fruits, intimating to them that to obey even in this small matter was better than sacrifice, and that, unless they were obedient, their offerings should not be accepted. It also taught them that the joy of harvest should express itself in charity to the poor, who must have their due out of what we have, as well as God his. Those that are truly sensible of the mercy they receive from God will without grudging show mercy to the poor.
entries.4f36733ef643e4064d275c2d25b1e94ce7d90dfc: <div eID="gen2601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2602" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">24</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, In the seventh month, in the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation. <hi type="super">25</hi> Ye shall do no servile work <hi type="italic">therein</hi>: but ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">26</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, 27 Also on the tenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of this seventh month <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> a day of atonement: it shall be an holy convocation unto you; and ye shall afflict your souls, and offer an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 28 And ye shall do no work in that same day: for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a day of atonement, to make an atonement for you before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">29</hi> For whatsoever soul <hi type="italic">it be</hi> that shall not be afflicted in that same day, he shall be cut off from among his people. <hi type="super">30</hi> And whatsoever soul <hi type="italic">it be</hi> that doeth any work in that same day, the same soul will I destroy from among his people. <hi type="super">31</hi> Ye shall do no manner of work: <hi type="italic">it shall be</hi> a statute for ever throughout your generations in all your dwellings. <hi type="super">32</hi> It <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> unto you a sabbath of rest, and ye shall afflict your souls: in the ninth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month at even, from even unto even, shall ye celebrate your sabbath. <div eID="gen2602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2603" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The institution of the feast of trumpets, on the first day of the seventh month, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.24-Lev.23.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. That which was now the seventh month had been reckoned the first month, and the year of jubilee was still to begin with this month (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.8">ch. xxv. 8</reference>), so that this was their new year's day. It was to be as their other yearly sabbaths, a day of holy rest—<hi type="italic">You shall do no servile work therein;</hi> and a day of holy work—<hi type="italic">You shall offer an offering to the Lord;</hi> concerning these particular directions were afterwards given, <reference osisRef="Num.29.1">Num. xxix. 1</reference>. That which is here made peculiar to this festival is that it was <hi type="italic">a memorial of blowing of trumpets.</hi> They blew the trumpet every new moon (<reference osisRef="Ps.81.3">Ps. lxxxi. 3</reference>), but in the new moon of the seventh month it was to be done with more than ordinary solemnity; for they began to blow at sun-rise and continued till sun-set. Now, 1. This is here said to be a <hi type="italic">memorial,</hi> perhaps of the sound of the trumpet upon mount Sinai when the law was given, which must never be forgotten. Some think that it was a memorial of the creation of the world, which is supposed to have been in autumn; for which reason this was, till now, the first month. The mighty word by which God made the world is called <hi type="italic">the voice of his thunder</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.7">Ps. civ. 7</reference>); fitly therefore was it commemorated by blowing of trumpets, or a memorial of <hi type="italic">shouting,</hi> as the Chaldee renders it; for, when the <hi type="italic">foundations of the earth were fastened, all the sons of God shouted for joy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.6-Job.38.7">Job xxxviii. 6, 7</reference>. 2. The Jewish writers suppose it to have a spiritual signification. Now at the beginning of the year they were called by this sound of trumpet to shake off their spiritual drowsiness, to search and try their ways, and to amend them: the day of atonement was the ninth day after this; and thus they were awakened to prepare for that day, by sincere and serious repentance, that it might be indeed to them a day of atonement. And they say, "The devout Jews exercised themselves more in good works between the feast of trumpets and the day of expiation than at any other time of the year." 3. It was typical of the preaching of the gospel, by which joyful sound souls were to be called in to serve God and keep a spiritual feast to him. The conversion of the nations to the faith of Christ is said to be by the <hi type="italic">blowing of a great trumpet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.13">Isa. xxvii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen2603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2604" type="x-p"/> II. A repetition of the law of the day of atonement, that is, so much of it as concerned the people. 1. They must on this day rest from all manner of work, and not only from servile works as on other annual festivals; it must be as strict a rest as that of the weekly sabbath, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.28">v. 28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.30">30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.31">31</reference>. The reason is: <hi type="italic">For it is a day of atonement.</hi> Note, The humbling of our souls for sin, and the making of our peace with God, is work that requires the whole man, and the closest application of mind imaginable, and all little enough. He that would do the work of a day of atonement in its day, as it should be done, had need lay aside the thoughts of every thing else. On that day God <hi type="italic">spoke peace unto his people, and unto his saints;</hi> and therefore they must lay aside all their worldly business, that they might the more clearly and the more reverently hear that voice of joy and gladness. Fasting days should be days of rest. 2. They must afflict their souls, and this upon pain of being cut off by the hand of God, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.27">v. 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.29">29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.32">32</reference>. They must mortify the body, and deny the appetites of it, in token of their sorrow for the sins they had committed, and the mortifying of their indwelling corruptions. Every soul must be afflicted, because every soul was polluted, and guilty before God; while none have fulfilled the law of innocency none are exempt from the law of repentance, besides that every man must sigh and cry for the <hi type="italic">abominations of the land.</hi> 3. The entire day must be observed: <hi type="italic">From even to even you shall afflict your souls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.32">v. 32</reference>), that is, "You shall begin your fast, and the expressions of your humiliation, in the <hi type="italic">ninth day of the month at even.</hi>" They were to leave off all their worldly labour, and compose themselves to the work of the day approaching, some time before sun-set on the ninth day, and not to take any food (except children and sick people) till after sun-set on the tenth day. Note, The eves of solemn days ought to be employed in solemn preparation. When work for God and our souls is to be done, we should not straiten ourselves in time for the doing of it; for how can we spend our time better? Of this sabbath the rule here given is to be understood: <hi type="italic">From even unto even shall you celebrate your sabbath.</hi>
entries.36626166b68ba3360760f5c21d2955f312cb6cbe: <div eID="gen2604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2605" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">34</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, The fifteenth day of this seventh month <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the feast of tabernacles <hi type="italic">for</hi> seven days unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">35</hi> On the first day <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work <hi type="italic">therein.</hi> <hi type="super">36</hi> Seven days ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : on the eighth day shall be an holy convocation unto you; and ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a solemn assembly; <hi type="italic">and</hi> ye shall do no servile work <hi type="italic">therein.</hi> <hi type="super">37</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the feasts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which ye shall proclaim <hi type="italic">to be</hi> holy convocations, to offer an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , a burnt offering, and a meat offering, a sacrifice, and drink offerings, every thing upon his day: <hi type="super">38</hi> Beside the sabbaths of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and beside your gifts, and beside all your vows, and beside all your freewill offerings, which ye give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">39</hi> Also in the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when ye have gathered in the fruit of the land, ye shall keep a feast unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> seven days: on the first day <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a sabbath, and on the eighth day <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a sabbath. <hi type="super">40</hi> And ye shall take you on the first day the boughs of goodly trees, branches of palm trees, and the boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook; and ye shall rejoice before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God seven days. <hi type="super">41</hi> And ye shall keep it a feast unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> seven days in the year. <hi type="italic">It shall be</hi> a statute for ever in your generations: ye shall celebrate it in the seventh month. <hi type="super">42</hi> Ye shall dwell in booths seven days; all that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths: <hi type="super">43</hi> That your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">44</hi> And Moses declared unto the children of Israel the feasts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen2605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2606" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The institution of the feast of tabernacles, which was one of the three great feasts at which all the males were bound to attend, and celebrated with more expressions of joy than any of them. <div eID="gen2606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2607" type="x-p"/> 1. As to the directions for regulating this feast, observe, (1.) It was to be observed <hi type="italic">on the fifteenth day of the seventh month</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">v. 34</reference>), but five days after the day of atonement. We may suppose, though they were not all bound to attend on the day of atonement, as on the three great festivals, yet that many of the devout Jews came up so many days before the feast of tabernacles as to enjoy the opportunity of attending on the day of atonement. Now, [1.] The afflicting of their souls on the day of atonement prepared them for the joy of the feast of tabernacles. The more we are grieved and humbled for sin, the better qualified we are for the comforts of the Holy Ghost. [2.] The joy of this feast recompensed them for the sorrow of that fast; for those that <hi type="italic">sow in tears</hi> shall <hi type="italic">reap in joy.</hi> (2.) It was to continue eight days, the first and last of which were to be observed as sabbaths, days of holy rest and holy convocations, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.35-Lev.23.36">v. 35, 36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.39">39</reference>. The sacrifices to be offered on these eight days we have a very large appointment of, <reference osisRef="Num.29.12-Num.29.39">Num. xxix. 12</reference>, &c. (3.) During the first seven days of this feast all the people were to leave their houses, and the women and children in them, and to dwell in booths made of the boughs of thick trees, particularly palm trees, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">v. 40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.42">42</reference>. The Jews make the taking of the branches to be a distinct ceremony from the making of the booths. It is said, indeed (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.15">Neh. viii. 15</reference>), that they <hi type="italic">made their booths of the branches of trees,</hi> which they might do, and yet use that further expression of joy, the carrying of palm-branches in their hands, which appears to have been a token of triumph upon other occasions (<reference osisRef="John.12.13">John xii. 13</reference>), and is alluded to, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>. The eighth day some make a distinct feast of itself, but it is called (<reference osisRef="John.7.37">John vii. 37</reference>) <hi type="italic">that great day of the feast;</hi> it was the day on which they returned from their booths, to settle again in their own houses. (4.) They were to <hi type="italic">rejoice before the Lord God</hi> during all the time of this feast, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">v. 40</reference>. The tradition of the Jews is that they were to express their joy by dancing, and singing hymns of praise to God, with musical instruments: and not the common people only, but the wise men of Israel, and their elders, were to do it in the court of the sanctuary: for (say they) the joy with which a man rejoices in doing a commandment is really a great service. <div eID="gen2607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2608" type="x-p"/> 2. As to the design of this feast, <div eID="gen2608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2609" type="x-p"/> (1.) It was to be kept in remembrance of their dwelling in tents in the wilderness. Thus it is expounded here (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">That your generations may know,</hi> not only by the written history, but by this ocular tradition, <hi type="italic">that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths.</hi> Thus it kept in perpetual remembrance, [1.] The meanness of their beginning, and the low and desolate state out of which God advanced that people. Note, Those that are comfortably fixed ought often to call to mind their former unsettled state, when they were but little in their own eyes. [2.] The mercy of God to them, that, when they dwelt in tabernacles, God not only set up a tabernacle for himself among them, but, with the utmost care and tenderness imaginable, hung a canopy over them, even the cloud that sheltered them from the heat of the sun. God's former mercies to us and our fathers ought to be kept in everlasting remembrance. The eighth day was the great day of this feast, because then they returned to their own houses again, and remembered how, after they had long dwelt in tents in the wilderness, at length they came to a happy settlement in the land of promise, where they dwelt in goodly houses. And they would the more sensibly value and be thankful for the comforts and conveniences of their houses when they had been seven days dwelling in booths. It is good for those that have ease and plenty sometimes to learn what it is to endure hardness. <div eID="gen2609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2610" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was a feast of in-gathering, so it is called, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Exod. xxiii. 16</reference>. When they had gathered in the <hi type="italic">fruit of their land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.39">v. 39</reference>), the vintage as well as the harvest, then they were to keep this feast in thankfulness to God for all the increase of the year; and some think that the eighth day of the feast had special reference to this ground of the institution. Note, The joy of harvest ought to be improved for the furtherance of our joy in God. <hi type="italic">The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof,</hi> and therefore whatever we have the comfort of, he must have the glory of, especially when any mercy is perfected. <div eID="gen2610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2611" type="x-p"/> (3.) It was a typical feast. It is supposed by many that our blessed Saviour was born much about the time of this feast; then he left his mansions of light above to <hi type="italic">tabernacle among us</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">John i. 14</reference>), and he dwelt in booths. And the worship of God under the New Testament is prophesied of under the notion of keeping the <hi type="italic">feast of tabernacles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zech. xiv. 16</reference>. For, [1.] The gospel of Christ teaches us to dwell in tabernacles, to sit loose to this world, as those that have here no continuing city, but by faith, and hope and holy contempt of present things, to <hi type="italic">go out to Christ without the camp,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.13-Heb.13.14">Heb. xiii. 13, 14</reference>. [2.] It teaches us to rejoice before the Lord our God. Those are the circumcision, Israelites indeed, that always <hi type="italic">rejoice in Christ Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Phil. iii. 3</reference>. And the more we are taken off from this world the less liable we are to the interruption of our joys. <div eID="gen2611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2612" type="x-p"/> II. The summary and conclusion of these institutions. <div eID="gen2612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2613" type="x-p"/> 1. God appointed these feasts (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.37-Lev.23.38">v. 37, 38</reference>), <hi type="italic">besides the sabbaths and your free-will offerings.</hi> This teaches us, (1.) That calls to extraordinary services will not excuse us from our constant stated performances. Within the days of the feast of tabernacles there must fall at least one sabbath, which must be as strictly observed as any other. (2.) That God's institutions leave room for free-will offerings. Not that we may invent what he never instituted, but we may repeat what he has instituted, ordinarily, the oftener the better. God is well pleased with a willing people. <div eID="gen2613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2614" type="x-p"/> 2. Moses declared them to the children of Israel, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.44">v. 44</reference>. He let them know what God appointed, and neither more nor less. Thus Paul delivered to the churches what he had <hi type="italic">received from the Lord.</hi> We have reason to be thankful that the feasts of the Lord, declared unto us, are not so numerous, nor the observance of them so burdensome and costly, as theirs then were, but more spiritual and significant, and surer sweeter earnests of the everlasting feast, at the last in-gathering, which we hope to be celebrating to eternity.  <chapter eID="Lev.23"/> <div eID="gen2614" type="x-p"/>

entries.53c42523c8b24a958bb7ed2703a3057040d4413e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1169"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.23.1-Lev.23.4">Le 23:1-4</reference>. Of Sundry Feasts.</title> <div sID="gen1600" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1169"/><hi type="bold">2. Speak unto the children of Israel, ... concerning the feasts of the Lord--</hi>literally, "the times of assembling, or solemnities" (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.20">Is 33:20</reference>); and this is a preferable rendering, applicable to all sacred seasons mentioned in this chapter, even the day of atonement, which was observed as a fast. They were appointed by the direct authority of God and announced by a public proclamation, which is called "the joyful sound" (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.15">Psa 89:15</reference>). Those "holy convocations" were evidences of divine wisdom, and eminently subservient to the maintenance and diffusion of religious knowledge and piety. <div eID="gen1600" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e47a91d15b2afac7b02facc220c4dd4ded9be8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1170"/><div sID="gen1601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1170"/><hi type="bold">3. Six days shall work be done: but the seventh day is the sabbath of rest--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Exod.20.8">Ex 20:8</reference>). The Sabbath has the precedence given to it, and it was to be "a holy convocation," observed by families "in their dwellings"; where practicable, by the people repairing to the door of the tabernacle; at later periods, by meeting in the schools of the prophets, and in synagogues. <div eID="gen1601" type="x-p"/>
entries.fdab8ffca719671a471c562de77dcda989167094: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1171"/><div sID="gen1602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1171"/><hi type="bold">4. These are the feasts of the Lord, which ye shall proclaim in their seasons--</hi>Their observance took place in the parts of the year corresponding to our March, May, and September. Divine wisdom was manifested in fixing them at those periods; in winter, when the days were short and the roads broken up, a long journey was impracticable; while in summer the harvest and vintage gave busy employment in the fields. Besides, another reason for the choice of those seasons probably was to counteract the influence of Egyptian associations and habits. And God appointed more sacred festivals for the Israelites in the month of September than the people of Egypt had in honor of their idols. These institutions, however, were for the most part prospective, the observance being not binding on the Israelites during their wanderings in the wilderness, while the regular celebration was not to commence till their settlement in Canaan. <div eID="gen1602" type="x-p"/>
entries.869766fec1ed9dfc0ee2171cf79bae16d6362259: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1172"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.23.5-Lev.23.8">Le 23:5-8</reference>. The Passover.</title> <div sID="gen1603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1172"/><hi type="bold">5. the Lord's passover--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Exod.12.2">Ex 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.18">14, 18</reference>). The institution of the passover was intended to be a perpetual memorial of the circumstances attending the redemption of the Israelites, while it had a typical reference to a greater redemption to be effected for God's spiritual people. On the first and last days of this feast, the people were forbidden to work [Le 23:7, 8]; but while on the Sabbath they were not to do any work, on feast days they were permitted to dress meat--and hence the prohibition is restricted to "no servile work." At the same time, those two days were devoted to "holy convocation"--special seasons of social devotion. In addition to the ordinary sacrifices of every day, there were to be "offerings by fire" on the altar (see <reference osisRef="Num.28.19">Nu 28:19</reference>), while unleavened bread was to be eaten in families all the seven days (see <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.8">1Co 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen1603" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6cd38cc18cb054819ea31869d1933860f845165: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1173"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.23.9-Lev.23.14">Le 23:9-14</reference>. The Sheaf of First Fruits.</title> <div sID="gen1604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1173"/><hi type="bold">10. ye shall bring a sheaf of the first-fruits of your harvest unto the priest--</hi>A sheaf, literally, an omer, of the first-fruits of the barley harvest. The barley being sooner ripe than the other grains, the reaping of it formed the commencement of the general harvest season. The offering described in this passage was made on the sixteenth of the first month, the day following the first Passover Sabbath, which was on the fifteenth (corresponding to the beginning of our April); but it was reaped after sunset on the previous evening by persons deputed to go with sickles and obtain samples from different fields. These, being laid together in a sheaf or loose bundle, were brought to the court of the temple, where the grain was winnowed, parched, and bruised in a mortar. Then, after some incense had been sprinkled on it, the priest waved the sheaf aloft before the Lord towards the four different points of the compass, took a part of it and threw it into the fire of the altar--all the rest being reserved to himself. It was a proper and beautiful act, expressive of dependence on the God of nature and providence--common among all people, but more especially becoming the Israelites, who owed their land itself as well as all it produced to the divine bounty. The offering of the wave-sheaf sanctified the whole harvest (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.16">Ro 11:16</reference>). At the same time, this feast had a typical character, and pre-intimated the resurrection of Christ (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">1Co 15:20</reference>), who rose from the dead on the very day the first-fruits were offered. <div eID="gen1604" type="x-p"/>
entries.164d2754ddbd530af379b0f82e2d6c8ccba46267: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1174"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.23.15-Lev.23.22">Le 23:15-22</reference>. Feast of Pentecost.</title> <div sID="gen1605" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1174"/><hi type="bold">15. ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath--</hi>that is, after the first day of the passover week, which was observed as a Sabbath. <div eID="gen1605" type="x-p"/>
entries.748d806e085b696383d4e50a571d1bfd39c31dac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1175"/><div sID="gen1606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1175"/><hi type="bold">16. number fifty days--</hi>The forty-ninth day after the presentation of the first-fruits, or the fiftieth, including it, was the feast of Pentecost. (See also <reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Ex 23:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.9">De 16:9</reference>). <div eID="gen1606" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c4ab4f0ce684051023f41d04aca752807552b8f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1176"/><div sID="gen1607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1176"/><hi type="bold">17. Ye shall bring out of your habitations two wave loaves of two tenth deals, &c.--</hi>These loaves were made of "fine" or wheaten flour, the quantity contained in them being somewhat more than ten pounds in weight. As the wave-sheaf gave the signal for the commencement, the two loaves solemnized the termination of the harvest season. They were the first-fruits of that season, being offered unto the Lord by the priest in name of the whole nation. (See <reference osisRef="Exod.34.22">Ex 34:22</reference>). The loaves used at the Passover were unleavened; those presented at Pentecost were leavened--a difference which is thus accounted for, that the one was a memorial of the bread hastily prepared at their departure, while the other was a tribute of gratitude to God for their daily food, which was leavened. <div eID="gen1607" type="x-p"/>
entries.be08a8273f4ab8e3f36296f7bf70fa8c503a26c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1177"/><div sID="gen1608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1177"/><hi type="bold">21. ye shall proclaim on the selfsame day, that it may be an holy convocation unto you: ye shall do no servile work therein--</hi>Though it extended over a week, the first day only was held as a Sabbath, both for the national offering of first-fruits and a memorial of the giving of the law. <div eID="gen1608" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c3af297ada9e061615eeba5614d78134d643be4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1178"/><div sID="gen1609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1178"/><hi type="bold">22. thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field when thou reapest, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.9">Le 19:9</reference>). The repetition of this law here probably arose from the priests reminding the people, at the presentation of the first-fruits, to unite piety to God with charity to the poor. <div eID="gen1609" type="x-p"/>
entries.b81c7f0219f064df82c044a7cb3cac60971ec1d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1179"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.23.23-Lev.23.25">Le 23:23-25</reference>. Feast of Trumpets.</title> <div sID="gen1610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1179"/><hi type="bold">24. In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath--</hi>That was the first day of the ancient civil year.<div eID="gen1610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a memorial of blowing of trumpets--</hi>Jewish writers say that the trumpets were sounded thirty successive times, and the reason for the institution was for the double purpose of announcing the commencement of the new year, which was (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.25">Le 23:25</reference>) to be religiously observed (see <reference osisRef="Num.29.3">Nu 29:3</reference>), and of preparing the people for the approaching solemn feast. <div eID="gen1611" type="x-p"/>
entries.05e46185a49b11e5ec74c4d64f9e7b93a5b1df64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1180"/><div sID="gen1612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1180"/><hi type="bold">27-32. there shall be a day of atonement ... and ye shall afflict your souls--</hi>an unusual festival, at which the sins of the whole year were expiated. (See <reference osisRef="Lev.16.29-Lev.16.34">Le 16:29-34</reference>). It is here only stated that the severest penalty was incurred by the violation of this day. <div eID="gen1612" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ea12f819ca4523b92086bd5124364d28b370c83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1181"/><div sID="gen1613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1181"/><hi type="bold">34-44. the feast of tabernacles, for seven days unto the Lord--</hi>This festival, which was instituted in grateful commemoration of the Israelites having securely dwelt in booths or tabernacles in the wilderness, was the third of the three great annual festivals, and, like the other two, it lasted a week. It began on the fifteenth day of the month, corresponding to the end of our September and beginning of October, which was observed as a Sabbath; and it could be celebrated only at the place of the sanctuary, offerings being made on the altar every day of its continuance. The Jews were commanded during the whole period of the festival to dwell in booths, which were erected on the flat roofs of houses, in the streets or fields; and the trees made use of are by some stated to be the citron, the palm, the myrtle, and the willow, while others maintain the people were allowed to take any trees they could obtain that were distinguished for verdure and fragrance. While the solid branches were reserved for the construction of the booths, the lighter branches were carried by men, who marched in triumphal procession, singing psalms and crying "Hosanna!" which signifies, "Save, we beseech thee!" (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.15">Psa 118:15</reference>, 25, 26). It was a season of great rejoicing. But the ceremony of drawing water from the pool, which was done on the last day, seems to have been the introduction of a later period (<reference osisRef="John.7.37">Joh 7:37</reference>). That last day was the eighth, and, on account of the scene at Siloam, was called "the great day of the feast." The feast of ingathering, when the vintage was over, was celebrated also on that day [Ex 23:16; 34:22], and, as the conclusion of one of the great festivals, it was kept as a sabbath. <chapter eID="Lev.23"/>

entries.a13552115f1311bbfe2fd3b8839ea7de35eb8c24: <div eID="gen4968" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4969" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4970" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4970" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4969" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4971" type="x-p"/> The feast of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.1">Lev 23:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.2">Lev 23:2</reference>. The Sabbath, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.3">Lev 23:3</reference>. The passover and unleavened bread, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.4-Lev.23.8">Lev 23:4-8</reference>. The feast of first-fruits, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.9-Lev.23.14">Lev 23:9-14</reference>. The feast of pentecost, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.15-Lev.23.21">Lev 23:15-21</reference>. Gleanings to be left for the poor, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.22">Lev 23:22</reference>. The feast of trumpets, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.23-Lev.23.25">Lev 23:23-25</reference>. The great day of atonement, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.26-Lev.23.32">Lev 23:26-32</reference>. The feast of tabernacles, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.33-Lev.23.44">Lev 23:33-44</reference>.
entries.3b44f0f4ddc76ceafafc7567875070ab6f920206: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen4971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4972" type="x-p"/> These are my feasts - The original word מועד moad is properly applied to any solemn anniversary, by which great and important ecclesiastical, political, or providential facts were recorded; see Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.1.14">Gen 1:14</reference> (note). Anniversaries of this kind were observed in all nations; and some of them, in consequence of scrupulously regular observation, became chronological epochs of the greatest importance in history: the Olympiads, for example.
entries.f605fced0cc9b2d042a9c7f64e601c15737dff8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen4972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4973" type="x-p"/> The seventh day is the Sabbath - This, because the first and greatest solemnity, is first mentioned. He who kept not this, in the most religious manner, was not capable of keeping any of the others. The religious observance of the Sabbath stands at the very threshold of all religion. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.2.3">Gen 2:3</reference>.
entries.dcf31c9c235e317b753b64f33c0f4be6ed3f1fa2: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen4973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4974" type="x-p"/> The Lord's passover - See this largely explained in the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.12.21-Exo.12.27">Exo 12:21-27</reference> (note).
entries.ea9b5d8e294e3ff0946aec190a7789280d0aeed6: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen4974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4975" type="x-p"/> He shalt wave the sheaf - He shall move it to and fro before the people, and thereby call their attention to the work of Divine Providence, and excite their gratitude to God for preserving to them the kindly fruits of the earth. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.27">Exo 29:27</reference>, and Exodus 7 at end.
entries.f76bb0acd7b4885a28e3b973d3302f51181f7bb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen4975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4976" type="x-p"/> Ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears - It is right that God, the dispenser of every blessing, should be acknowledged as such, and the first-fruits of the field, etc., dedicated to him. Concerning the dedication of the first-fruits, see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.22.29">Exo 22:29</reference>. Parched ears of corn and green ears, fried, still constitute a part, and not a disagreeable one, of the food of the Arabs now resident in the Holy Land. See Hasselquist.
entries.9510192939a276255a189b3338762af059adc738: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen4976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4977" type="x-p"/> Ye shall count unto you - seven Sabbaths - That is, from the sixteenth of the first month to the sixth of the third month. These seven weeks, called here Sabbaths, were to be complete, i. e., the forty-nine days must be finished, and the next day, the fiftieth, is what, from the Septuagint, we call pentecost. See the note on <reference osisRef="Luk.6.1">Luk 6:1</reference>.
entries.e0db0f694d049ea800f8d381d39cf5016bab09e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen4977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4978" type="x-p"/> Neither shalt thou gather any gleaning - See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.9">Lev 19:9</reference>.
entries.be49815a441680f477d584106b171ca6683ceed9: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen4978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4979" type="x-p"/> A memorial of blowing of trumpets - This is generally called the feast of trumpets; and as it took place on the first day of the seventh month, Tisri, which answers to September, which month was the commencement of what was called the civil year, the feast probably had no other design than to celebrate the commencement of that year, if indeed such a distinction obtained among the ancient Jews. See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.12.2">Exo 12:2</reference>. Some think creation began at this time.
entries.b1c2bd2bf743556951d3191b24849fc1df3bb97d: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen4979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4980" type="x-p"/> A day of atonement - See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.16.2">Lev 16:2</reference>, etc., where this subject is largely explained.
entries.38d133f382db3fb7b54aab10216d27eccfa01e34: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen4980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4981" type="x-p"/> The feast of tabernacles - In this solemnity the people left their houses, and dwelt in booths or tents made of the branches of goodly trees and thick trees, (of what kind the text does not specify), together with palm-trees and willows of the brook, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">Lev 23:40</reference>. And in these they dwelt seven days, in commemoration of their forty years' sojourning and dwelling in tents in the wilderness while destitute of any fixed habitations. In imitation of this feast among the people of God, the Gentiles had their feasts of tents. Plutarch speaks particularly of feasts of this kind in honor of Bacchus, and thinks from the custom of the Jews in celebrating the feast of tabernacles, that they worshipped the god Bacchus, "because he had a feast exactly of the same kind called the feast of tabernacles, Σκηνη, which they celebrated in the time of vintage, bringing tables out into the open air furnished with all kinds of fruit, and sitting under tents made of vine branches and ivy." - Plut. Symp., lib. iv., Q. 6. According to Ovid the feast of Anna Perenna was celebrated much in the same way. Some remained in the open air, others formed to themselves tents and booths made of branches of trees, over which they spread garments, and kept the festival with great rejoicings. "Sub Jove pars durat; pauci tentoria ponunt; <div eID="gen4981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4982" type="x-p"/> Sunt, quibus e ramis frondea facta easa est. <div eID="gen4982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4983" type="x-p"/> Pars sibi pro rigidis calamos statuere columnis; <div eID="gen4983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4984" type="x-p"/> Desuper extentas imposuere togas." <div eID="gen4984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4985" type="x-p"/> Ovid, Fast., lib. ill. <div eID="gen4985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4986" type="x-p"/> Concerning this feast of tabernacles, see the note on <reference osisRef="Joh.7.37">Joh 7:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.38">Joh 7:38</reference>; and for the various feasts among the Jews, See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.23.14">Exo 23:14</reference>.
entries.91a2820c1d630780a1aea15792262941bdb3ecc3: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen4986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4987" type="x-p"/> Boughs of goodly trees - The Jews and many critics imagine the citron-tree to be intended, and by boughs of thick tree the myrtle.
entries.f42e810161f858432c7cc526b0ce3dba30b8fc99: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen4987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4988" type="x-p"/> That your generations may know, etc. - By the institution of this feast God had two great objects in view: <div eID="gen4988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4989" type="x-p"/> 1. To perpetuate the wonderful display of his providence and grace in bringing them out of Egypt, and in preserving them in the wilderness. <div eID="gen4989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4990" type="x-p"/> 2. To excite and maintain in them a spirit of gratitude and obedience, by leading them to consider deeply the greatness of the favors which they had received from his most merciful hands. <div eID="gen4990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4991" type="x-p"/> Signal displays of the mercy, kindness, and providential care of God should be particularly remembered. When we recollect that we deserve nothing at his hands, and that the debt of gratitude is all the debt we can pay, in it we should be cheerful, fervent, and frequent. An ungrateful heart is an unfeeling, unloving, unbelieving, and disobedient heart. Reader, pray to God that he may deliver thee from its influence and its curse.  <chapter eID="Lev.23"/> <div eID="gen4991" type="x-p"/>

entries.d8f582c601c1299cebadc54f85a85eb4223902fc: <reference osisRef="Lev.23.1-Lev.23.2">Lev 23:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen1469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1470" type="x-p"/> This chapter does not contain a “calendar of feasts,” or a summary and completion of the directions previously given in a scattered form concerning the festal times of Israel, but simply a list of those festal days and periods of the year at which holy meetings were to be held. This is most clearly stated in the heading (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.2">Lev 23:2</reference>): “<hi type="italic">the festal times of Jehovah, which ye shall call out as holy meetings, these are they, My feasts,</hi>” i.e., those which are to be regarded as My feasts, sanctified to Me. The festal seasons and days were called “feasts of Jehovah,” times appointed and fixed by Jehovah (see <reference osisRef="Gen.1.14">Gen 1:14</reference>), not because the feasts belonged to fixed times regulated by the course of the moon (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>), but because Jehovah had appointed them as days, or times, which were to be sanctified to Him. Hence the expression is not only used with reference to the Sabbath, the new moon, and the other yearly feasts; but in Num 28:2 and Num 29:39 it is extended so as to include the times of the daily morning and evening sacrifice. (On the “holy convocation” see Exo 12:16.)
entries.aae637f4777c290693ff99e647d8f1a3c92b0647: <reference osisRef="Lev.23.3">Lev 23:3</reference> <div eID="gen1470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1471" type="x-p"/> At the head of these <hi type="italic">moadim</hi> stood the <hi type="italic">Sabbath</hi>, as the day which God had already sanctified as a day of rest for His people, by His own rest on the seventh creation-day (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.3">Gen 2:3</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.20.8-Exod.20.11">Exo 20:8-11</reference>). On שׁבּתון שׁבּת, see at <reference osisRef="Exod.31.15">Exo 31:15</reference> and Exo 16:33. As a weekly returning day of rest, the observance of which had its foundation in the creative work of God, the Sabbath was distinguished from the yearly feasts, in which Israel commemorated the facts connected with its elevation into a people of God, and which were generally called “feasts of Jehovah” in the stricter sense, and as such were distinguished from the Sabbath (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.37">Lev 23:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.38">Lev 23:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13-Isa.1.14">Isa 1:13-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.31">1Ch 23:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.3">2Ch 31:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.10.34">Neh 10:34</reference>). This distinction is pointed out in the heading, “<hi type="italic">these are the feasts of Jehovah</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.4">Lev 23:4</reference>).<note placement="foot">Partly on account of his repetition, and partly because of the supposed discrepancy observable in the fact, that holy meetings are not prescribed for the Sabbath in the list of festal sacrifices in Num 28 and 29, <hi type="italic">Hupfield</hi> and <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> maintain that the words of <reference osisRef="Lev.23.2">Lev 23:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.23.3">Lev 23:3</reference>, from יהוה to מושׁבתיכם, notwithstanding their Elohistic expression, were not written by the Elohist, but are an interpolation of the later editor. The repetition of the heading, however, cannot prove anything at all with the constant repetitions that occur in the so-called Elohistic groundwork, especially as it can be fully explained by the reason mentioned in the text. And the pretended discrepancy rests upon the perfectly arbitrary assumption, that Num 28 and 29 contain a complete codex of all the laws relating to all the feasts. How totally this assumption is at variance with the calendar of feasts, is clear enough from the fact, that no rule is laid down there for the observance of the Sabbath, with the exception of the sacrifices to be offered upon it, and that even rest from labour is not commanded. Moreover <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> is wrong in identifying the “holy convocation” with a journey to the sanctuary, whereas appearance at the tabernacle to hold the holy convocations (for worship) was not regarded as necessary either in the law itself or according to the later orthodox custom, but, on the contrary, holy meetings for edification were held on the Sabbath in every place in the land, and it was out of this that the synagogues arose.</note> <div eID="gen1471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1472" type="x-p"/> In Num 28:11 the feast of new moon follows the Sabbath; but this is passed over here, because the new moon was not to be observed either with sabbatical rest or a holy meeting. <div eID="gen1472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1473" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lev.23.4">Lev 23:4</reference> contains the special heading for the yearly feasts. בּמועדם at their appointed time.
entries.681feeaeaf29e94a270783a6d46d384c6f1e17c2: <reference osisRef="Lev.23.5-Lev.23.14">Lev 23:5-14</reference> <div eID="gen1473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1474" type="x-p"/> The leading directions for the <hi type="italic">Passover</hi> and <hi type="italic">feast of Mazzoth</hi> are repeated from <reference osisRef="Exod.12.6">Exo 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.11">Exo 12:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.15">Exo 12:15</reference>-20. עבדה מלאכת, occupation of a work, signifies labour at some definite occupation, e.g., the building of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.24">Exo 35:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.36.1">Exo 36:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.36.3">Exo 36:3</reference>; hence occupation in connection with trade or one’s social calling, such as agriculture, handicraft, and so forth; whilst מלאכה is the performance of any kind of work, e.g., kindling fire for cooking food (<reference osisRef="Exod.35.2-Exod.35.3">Exo 35:2-3</reference>). On the Sabbath and the day of atonement every kind of civil work was prohibited, even to the kindling of fire for the purpose of cooking (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.3">Lev 23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.30">Lev 23:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.31">Lev 23:31</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.20.10">Exo 20:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.31.14">Exo 31:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.35.2-Exod.35.3">Exo 35:2-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.14">Deu 5:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.16.29">Lev 16:29</reference>; Num 29:7); on the other feast-days with a holy convocation, only servile work (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.7">Lev 23:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.8">Lev 23:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.21">Lev 23:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.25">Lev 23:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.35">Lev 23:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.36">Lev 23:36</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.12.16">Exo 12:16</reference>, and the explanation on <reference osisRef="Lev.12.1-Lev.12.8">Lev 12:1-8</reference> :15ff., and Num 28:18, Num 28:25-26; Num 29:1, Num 29:12, Num 29:35). To this there is appended a fresh regulation in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.9-Lev.23.14">Lev 23:9-14</reference>, with the repetition of the introductory clause, “<hi type="italic">And the Lord spake,</hi>” etc. When the Israelites had come into the land to be given them by the Lord, and had reaped the harvest, they were to bring a sheaf as first-fruits of their harvest to the priest, that he might wave it before Jehovah on the day after the Sabbath, i.e., after the first day of <hi type="italic">Mazzoth</hi>. According to <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Philo</hi>, it was a sheaf of barley; but this is not expressly commanded, because it would be taken for granted in Canaan, where the harvest began with the barley. In the warmer parts of Palestine the barley ripens about the middle of April, and is reaped in April or the beginning of May, whereas the wheat ripens two or three weeks later (<hi type="italic">Seetzen; </hi> Robinson<hi type="italic">'s Pal.</hi> ii. 263, 278). The priest was to wave the sheaf before Jehovah, i.e., to present it symbolically to Jehovah by the ceremony of waving, without burning any of it upon the altar. The rabbinical rule, viz., to dry a portion of the ears by the fire, and then, after rubbing them out, to burn them on the altar, was an ordinance of the later scribes, who knew not the law, and was based upon Lev 2:14. For the law in <reference osisRef="Lev.2.14">Lev 2:14</reference> refers to the offerings of first-fruits made by private persons, which are treated of in Num 18:12-13, and Deu 26:2. The sheaf of first-fruits, on the other hand, which was to be offered before Jehovah as a wave-offering in the name of the congregation, corresponded to the two wave-loaves which were leavened and then baked, and were to be presented to the Lord as first-fruits (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.17">Lev 23:17</reference>). As no portion of these wave-loaves was burned upon the altar, because nothing leavened was to be placed upon it (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.11">Lev 2:11</reference>), but they were assigned entirely to the priests, we have only to assume that the same application was intended by the law in the case of the sheaf of first-fruits, since the text only prescribes the waving, and does not contain a word about roasting, rubbing, or burning the grains upon the altar. השּׁבּת מחרת (the morrow after the Sabbath) signifies the next day after the first day of the feast of Mazzoth, i.e., the 16th Abib (<hi type="italic">Nisan</hi>), not the day of the Sabbath which fell in the seven days’ feast of Mazzoth, as the Baethoseans supposed, still less the 22nd of Nisan, or the day after the conclusion of the seven days’ feast, which always closed with a Sabbath, as <hi type="italic">Hitzig</hi> imagines.<note placement="foot">The view advocated by the Baethoseans, which has been lately supported by <hi type="italic">W. Schultz</hi>, is refuted not only by <reference osisRef="Josh.5.11">Jos 5:11</reference>, but by the definite article used, השּׁבּת, which points back to one of the feast-days already mentioned, and still more decisively by the circumstance, that according to <reference osisRef="Lev.23.15">Lev 23:15</reference> the seven weeks, at the close of which the feast of Pentecost was to be kept, were to be reckoned from this Sabbath; and if the Sabbath was not fixed, but might fall upon any day of the seven days’ feast of Mazzoth, and therefore as much as give or six days after the Passover, the feast of Passover itself would be forced out of the fundamental position which it occupied in the series of annual festivals (cf. <hi type="italic">Ranke</hi>, Pentateuch ii. 108). <hi type="italic">Hitzig's</hi> hypothesis has been revived by <hi type="italic">Hupfeld</hi> and <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, without any notice of the conclusive refutation given to it by <hi type="italic">Bδhr</hi> and <hi type="italic">Wieseler</hi>; only <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> makes “the Sabbath” not the concluding but the opening Sabbath of the feast of Passover, on the ground that “otherwise the festal sheaf would not have been offered till the 22nd of the month, and therefore would have come <hi type="italic">post festum</hi>.” But this hypothesis, which renders it necessary that the commencement of the ecclesiastical year should always be assigned to a Saturday (Sabbath), in order to gain weekly Sabbaths for the 14th and 21st of the month, as the opening and close of the feast of Passover, gives such a form to the Jewish year as would involve its invariably closing with a broken week; a hypothesis which is not only incapable of demonstration, but, from the holiness attached to the Jewish division of weeks, is <hi type="italic">a priori</hi> improbable, and in fact inconceivable. The Mosaic law, which gave such sanctity to the division of time into weeks, as founded upon the history of creation, by the institution of the observance of the Sabbath, that it raised the Sabbath into the groundwork of a magnificent festal cycle, could not possibly have made such an arrangement with regard to the time for the observance of the Passover, as would involve almost invariably the mutilation of the last week of the year, and an interruption of the old and sacred weekly cycle with the Sabbath festival at its close. The arguments by which so forced a hypothesis is defended, must be very conclusive indeed, to meet with any acceptance. But neither <hi type="italic">Hitzig</hi> nor his followers have been able to adduce any such arguments as these. Besides the word “Sabbath” and <reference osisRef="Josh.5.11">Jos 5:11</reference>, which prove nothing at all, the only other argument adduced by <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> is, that “it is impossible to see why precisely the second day of the <hi type="italic">azyma</hi>, when the people went about their ordinary duties, and there was no meeting at the sanctuary, should have been distinguished by the sacrificial gift which was the peculiar characteristic of the feast,” - an argument based upon the fallacious principle, that anything for which I can see no reason, cannot possibly have occurred.</note> <div eID="gen1474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1475" type="x-p"/> The “Sabbath” does not mean the seventh day of the week, but the day of rest, although the weekly Sabbath was always the seventh or last day of the week; hence not only the seventh day of the week (<reference osisRef="Exod.31.15">Exo 31:15</reference>, etc.), but the day of atonement (the tenth of the seventh month), is called “<hi type="italic">Sabbath</hi>,” and “<hi type="italic">Shabbath</hi> <hi type="italic">shabbathon</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.32">Lev 23:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.16.31">Lev 16:31</reference>). As a day of rest, on which no laborious work was to be performed (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.8">Lev 23:8</reference>), the first day of the feast of <hi type="italic">Mazzoth</hi> is called “<hi type="italic">Sabbath</hi>,” irrespectively of the day of the week upon which it fell; and “<hi type="italic">the morrow after the Sabbath</hi>” is equivalent to “the morrow after the Passover” mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.5.11">Jos 5:11</reference>, where “Passover” signifies the day at the beginning of which the paschal meal was held, i.e., the first day of unleavened bread, which commenced on the evening of the 14th, in other words, the 15th Abib. By offering the sheaf of first-fruits of the harvest, the Israelites were to consecrate their daily bread to the Lord their God, and practically to acknowledge that they owed the blessing of the harvest to the grace of God. They were not to eat any bread or roasted grains of the new corn till they had presented the offering of their God (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.14">Lev 23:14</reference>). This offering was fixed for the second day of the feast of the Passover, that the connection between the harvest and the Passover might be kept in subordination to the leading idea of the Passover itself (see at Exo 12:15.). But as the sheaf was not burned upon the altar, but only presented symbolically to the Lord by waving, and then handed over to the priests, an altar-gift had to be connected with it, - namely, a yearling sheep as a burnt-offering, a meat-offering of two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, and a drink-offering of a quarter of a hin of wine, - to give expression to the obligation and willingness of the congregation not only to enjoy their earthly food, but to strengthen all the members of their body for growth in holiness and diligence in good works.
